specAnchors.text: describe the difference between contamination and irradiation

primer.text: Two words, one trap. Irradiation bathes an object in radiation from outside — the object never becomes radioactive. Contamination puts radioactive atoms onto or into the material itself — and then it is radioactive. Protection differs for each, and the exam tests the difference.

modules.title: Contamination versus irradiation
modules.opening: Contamination is the unwanted arrival of radioactive material on or inside a substance — an accident, such as a leak — and the material becomes radioactive as a result. Irradiation is the deliberate exposure of a material to ionising radiation: useful for sterilisation, and it never makes the material radioactive.
keyPoints: Contamination is the unwanted transfer of radioactive material onto or into something.
A contaminated object becomes radioactive because it now contains a source.
Irradiation is exposing a material to ionising radiation, usually deliberately.
Irradiation does not make the exposed object radioactive.
Irradiation can still kill living cells — sterility comes at a dose.

low.restatement: Spill isotope on the bench: contaminated. Shine gamma at the bench: irradiated, but wipe-clean ordinary matter either way.
low.analogy: Contamination is spilling paint ON you; irradiation is standing in the spray of a paint gun — wet paint only where it lands as matter.
low.examPointer: The money sentence: only contamination makes things radioactive — irradiation never does.

medium.restatement: The distinction is about location of the source: outside the object (irradiation) versus part of the object (contamination). Consequences follow: irradiation stops when the beam stops, contamination persists and emits until the isotope decays or is removed.
medium.analogy: Sunlight warms you only while you stand in it (irradiation); a charcoal briquette in your pocket keeps burning wherever you go (contamination).
medium.examPointer: Comparison tables on this pair are frequent — rehearse description/source/prevention/causes rows.

modules.title: Protection and the comparison
modules.opening: Irradiation risk falls with time, distance and shielding; contamination risk falls with airtight barriers and careful handling, because blocking an internal emitter is impossible. Inside the body, contamination is the graver hazard — the source rides with you.
keyPoints: Irradiation exposure is reduced by minimising time and maximising distance from the source.
Contamination is prevented by airtight suits and safe handling, not by shielding after the fact.
Inhaled or ingested sources — radon gas, contaminated food — irradiate the internal organs from inside.
Contamination is generally the greater risk; irradiation is usually deliberate and controlled.
Long-half-life sources pose the greater contamination risk — the long-term burden that waste policy must carry.

low.restatement: Beam hazard: step back, hurry up, hide behind lead. Spill hazard: seal up, gloves on, never touch — you cannot shield what is already inside.
low.analogy: Irradiation is standing near a bonfire — move away. Contamination is a lit match in your pocket — distance is no longer available.
low.examPointer: Match each protection to its hazard; swapping them is the classic lost mark.

medium.restatement: The half-life asymmetry explains the risk table: high activity (short half-life) means intense irradiation now, while longevity (long half-life) means a contamination burden that persists for storage lifetimes. Hence waste policy favours long-term geological isolation, and laboratory policy favours tongs and short exposures.
medium.analogy: A short-half-life source is a firework — fierce but brief; a long-half-life source is a slow candle — gentle but it stays lit for years.
medium.examPointer: WE-style questions ask for the half-life risk split: short → irradiation, long → contamination.

glossary.definition: The accidental transfer of a radioactive substance onto or into a material.
Exposing a material to ionising radiation without it becoming radioactive.
Protective clothing that prevents radioactive atoms reaching the skin or being inhaled.
Short half-lives dominate irradiation risk; long half-lives dominate contamination risk.
